locations.anchor: Removing Ia feedback eliminated detected cycles in the tested production configuration
locations.source_line: The Gait2392-based evaluations use the same reference-library and pathway-removal procedures to compare alternative neural organizations. The full graded, pruned, six-synergy, and W2L-layout configurations show different responses to feedback removal and different agreement with the tuning and library references. Removing Ia feedback eliminated detected cycles in the tested production configuration, whereas other removals and other network organizations had different effects. The library comparisons also exposed asymmetric activity and limited transfer beyond the tuning reference (Appendix~\ref{sec:gait_library_results}). This demonstrates that the models and experiment drivers can discriminate controller dependence and transfer limits; the comparison does not establish normal human gait.

The 43-cycle library contains 32 running trials from eight subjects at four speeds, ten walking references, and a predicted-walking cycle. The walking references span prescribed speeds of \qtyrange{0.5}{2.0}{\meter\per\second} and self-selected trials. The production network (\texttt{s3k}), reduced-connection network (\texttt{s3kpruned}), six-group activation network (\texttt{syn6}), and W2L-organization network (\texttt{w2lvar}) were scored without treating a good tuning-reference score as evidence of generalization. Library scores were substantially more negative (Table~\ref{tab:gait_sweep}), and the evaluations showed unilateral or asymmetric gait. This comparison bounds transfer to the available references; it does not validate normal human walking.

The 262-neuron controller receives 230 inputs and drives 54 reference-tension actuators. Its MN target-current compensation cancels incoming PF and reflex synaptic currents to track the force allocator's targets. Consequently, the effective comparison concerns RG timing, engineered force allocation, and mechanical response, rather than normal PF/reflex authority over activation. Toe-out and small post-ramp knee excursions remain, and the stepping acceptance tests fail.

locations.anchor: disabling all sensory feedback shifted median bilateral contact phase from 0.498 to 0.223 cycles.
locations.source_line: The saved W2L controller was tested with all saved effective gains delivered to the compiled network. With controller, drive, and support settings fixed, disabling all sensory feedback shifted median bilateral contact phase from 0.498 to 0.223 cycles. A phase of 0.5 cycles indicates alternating foot loading; the supported-stepping criterion accepts 0.35--0.65 cycles. Forward progression and joint cycling persisted, but the feedback-disabled condition failed this criterion for supported stepping (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_ablation_pair}). Over the \qtyrange{4.5}{30}{\second} scored window, forward displacement was \qty{2.239}{\meter} with feedback and \qty{1.996}{\meter} without it. Thus, the demonstrated feedback contribution is to bilateral contact coordination, rather than the existence of oscillation or forward motion. Additional pathway deletions and stimulus tests are summarized in Appendix~\ref{sec:app_w2l_perturbations} (Figure~\ref{fig:app_w2l_perturbations}).\par

locations.anchor: The primary deliverable is SADb Explorer,
locations.source_line: The primary deliverable is SADb Explorer, a browser application containing 1,393 literature and related records. It has four main tabs (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_clusters}, callout~(A)): Table searches individual records, Pivot compares classifications, Bubble map explores citation links among papers, and Search (online) finds candidate additions through OpenAlex. The records, notes, and citation graph are embedded in the application, so the first three tabs can be used without an internet connection. Search (online) requires an internet connection and lets the user save candidate records for later curation. The application preserves both the records retained for active curation and archived records from the collected material.

Source-access limitations are recorded with the shortlist; inclusion and classification decisions remain manual.

locations.anchor: The resource and the evaluation of AI-assisted literature curation were presented
locations.source_line: The Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) is a curated literature resource for studying sensory feedback in locomotion and posture. It links findings from animal and human studies to afferent classes, feedback pathways, and computational models. I developed it within the AARL's NeuroNex Communication, Coordination, and Control in Nervous Systems (C3NS) effort. The resource and the evaluation of AI-assisted literature curation were presented at Neuroscience 2023 and 2024, respectively \citep{bolen_sensory_2023,bolen_using_2024}.

The placement search varies actuator attachments to control moment arm and muscle excursion over the joint range of motion \citep{bolen_determination_2019,morrow_optimization_2020}. For the erector spinae, internal oblique, and external oblique at the lumbosacral joint, the targets are Gait2392 torque surfaces sampled at 100 positions along each of two joint coordinates.

locations.anchor: The original cost combined the summed absolute torque mismatch
locations.source_line: The original cost combined the summed absolute torque mismatch over the sampled poses, actuator length, displacement of the attachments from their starting locations, and a diameter-dependent penalty. The published weights for the first three terms were $10^{-4}$, $10^{-2}$, and $1$, respectively; the penalties for \qtylist{10;20;40}{\mm} BPAs were $1$, $5$, and $15$. These were numerical weights chosen to balance differently scaled cost terms. The geometric terms discouraged impractical placements but did not impose collision avoidance: attachments could lie away from the modeled bones, and routes could intersect them. This study established the placement-search approach; it did not establish physical torque accuracy or satisfaction of the human torque requirement at every pose.

locations.anchor: The identification proceeded in two stages.
locations.source_line: The identification proceeded in two stages. The flexor stage fits the two-bracket model $(\chi_{0}, \chi_{1}, \chi_{2})$ across the four pinned-knee flexor tests, with the $l_{0}=\qty{48.5}{\cm}$ and \qty{41.0}{\cm} tests in training and the $l_{0}=\qty{45.7}{\cm}$ and \qty{40.6}{\cm} tendon tests held out for validation. It evolved a population of 150 for up to 600 generations, terminating early once the relative change in the spread of the Pareto front fell below $4\times10^{-3}$. The extensor stage locks $(\chi_{1}, \chi_{2})$ to a member of the flexor Pareto front, enforcing a single stiffness pair across configurations, and solves only the extensor-specific terms $(\chi_{0}, \chi_{3})$ on a six-test pool of the pinned-extensor campaign, at resting lengths of \qty{40.0}{\cm} plain and with tendon, \qty{43.6}{\cm}, \qty{43.2}{\cm} with tendon, \qty{45.7}{\cm}, and \qty{46.5}{\cm}, with the \qty{43.6}{\cm}, \qty{43.2}{\cm}-tendon, and \qty{45.7}{\cm} tests in training and the \qty{40.0}{\cm} plain, \qty{40.0}{\cm}-tendon, and \qty{46.5}{\cm} tests held out for validation, and the extensor offset allowed negative values. The refit used a population of 50 for up to 150 generations at a spread tolerance of $1\times10^{-3}$. Both stages searched a normalized space, with length offsets in centimeters and stiffnesses on a base-ten logarithmic scale, so that the genetic search samples the decade-spanning stiffness bounds uniformly. Expressed in physical units, the flexor bounds were $\chi_{0} \in [0, 20]$~\si{\milli\metre}, $\chi_{1} \in [3\times10^{4}, 10^{6}]$~\si{\N\per\metre}, and $\chi_{2} \in [5\times10^{3}, 2\times10^{4}]$~\si{\N\per\metre}; the extensor refit searched $\chi_{0} \in [-20, +5]$~\si{\milli\metre} and $\chi_{3} \in [0, 1]$ with the stiffness pair locked. The initial flexor population was drawn from $\chi_{0} \in [5, 15]$~\si{\milli\metre}, $\chi_{1} \in [5\times10^{4}, 5\times10^{5}]$, and $\chi_{2} \in [7\times10^{3}, 1.5\times10^{4}]$~\si{\N\per\metre}.

locations.anchor: together with the first hardware torque measurements of the redesigned extensor route.
locations.source_line: Artificial muscles such as braided pneumatic actuators (BPAs) reproduce the force and contraction behavior of skeletal muscle, making them attractive for the legs of musculoskeletal robots. However, the isometric torque a BPA delivers about a joint remains difficult to predict, because rigid-body torque models omit attachment compliance, effective-length offsets, and the contraction lost where the actuator wraps over the joint. In this work, we measured isometric knee torque on pinned and biomimetic knee test stands across actuator resting lengths, isolated error sources with a hybrid torque calculation, and identified correction terms by multiobjective optimization. Our analysis resulted in (1) a corrected torque model whose length offset, effective stiffness, and fictive-strain wrapping loss, expressed through the unloaded \qty{620}{\kPa} contraction, reduce held-out prediction error on both pinned-knee test families and are evaluated on the biomimetic knee; (2) one effective stiffness pair shared across flexor and extensor configurations; and (3) redesigned attachment routes that meet or exceed human isometric knee-torque targets with quantified margins, together with the first hardware torque measurements of the redesigned extensor route. The optimized model and redesign pipeline support first-iteration torque design of BPA-actuated robot joints.

locations.section: Paper §4.3.2 Physical Validation Against Human Torque
locations.anchor: Both redesigned routes met or exceeded their selected human-muscle torque references
A hybrid calculation isolated the error sources,
locations.source_line: Isometric knee torque is the product of the force an actuator develops and the moment arm of its line of action about the joint axis, and the force itself is set by the actuator's effective length through the force model. Each link in that chain is a design quantity: the attachment routing fixes the moment arm, the resting length and attachment compliance set the effective contraction, and wrapping over the joint removes usable length. We built two knee test stands, measured isometric torque across each joint's range of motion (RoM) with \qtylist{10;20}{\mm} Festo braided pneumatic actuators (BPAs) in flexor and extensor configurations, and compared the measurements against the original rigid-body model, the improved actuator force characterization alone, and the optimized model developed here. A hybrid calculation isolated the error sources, a multiobjective identification produced the correction terms, and the optimized model then drove a redesign of the attachment routes against human isometric torque targets.
